patch.value: Behavioural constants are undeclared and unlabelled: every threshold, cap, half-life and default was fitted to this one corpus and nothing states which of them are principled

Every behavioural constant in the product was chosen while looking at one corpus, and nothing declares which of them are principled and which were fitted. The tool promises to serve a scratch workspace of a few items spanning minutes and an archive of millions spanning decades, and to be customizable to domains that are not software project management, and it makes that promise while its tuning is invisible.

The population, sampled from the live build. A file-list worklist truncates at 40. Graph centrality bounds at 10 and the next-recommendation slate at 5. Default token budgets, recency half-lives and decay weights are chosen numbers, one of which - the recency weight of 0.35 tied for largest - is already recorded elsewhere as a behavioural hazard. The static quality gate caps a file at 3,400 non-blank non-comment lines. Duplicate detection uses a jaccard threshold and scores an issue-code match at 0.99. Stale-path classification caps move candidates at 3. Search relevance is graded against a golden-query set drawn from this project's own vocabulary. None of these is wrong today. All of them are unlabelled.

Why unlabelled is the defect rather than any particular value. A constant fitted to this corpus is not merely suboptimal on a different one; it is silently suboptimal, because the output shape is identical and nothing signals that a bound was chosen against a different population. A worklist that samples 3 percent of a corpus renders exactly like one that samples all of it. A half-life tuned to a seven-month project makes a decade-old archive uniformly stale, and the staleness looks like data rather than like tuning. A golden-query set drawn from one vocabulary certifies retrieval for that vocabulary alone. The existing discipline around hierarchy depth is the model to generalize: the observation that depth maxes at 6 is recorded explicitly as a fact about this corpus that must never be manufactured elsewhere. That care has been applied to exactly one number.

What this item delivers. An inventory of every numeric constant that affects behaviour, declared as data rather than embedded as a literal, each carrying its unit, where it came from, and one of three labels. Invariant means it follows from a stated principle and does not depend on the corpus. Calibrated means it was fitted, and the fitting procedure and the corpus are recorded and repeatable. Arbitrary means it was chosen and nobody has checked, which is an honest label that most of the population will start with. On top of the inventory, one rule: an arbitrary constant may govern a presentation default but may not be load-bearing on a correctness claim. And one gate: a new numeric literal on a behavioural path must arrive with a label, so the population stops growing while the existing members are dispositioned. That is the same ratchet shape this project has already used successfully for import boundaries, coverage and token cost.

Scope boundary. This item declares and gates the constants. It does not retune any of them, and it does not build the multi-scale corpus suite that would let them be retuned - that stays with the scale conformance work. It does not cover non-numeric defaults such as enum choices or default output formats, which are contract questions owned elsewhere. It does not cover coverage or lint thresholds that gate the build rather than the product's behaviour, except to record them as out of scope with a reason, because the distinction between a gate constant and a behaviour constant is itself part of what the inventory has to make explicit.

value.text: Duplicate check before create: pm-cstl is CLOSED and made ONE threshold configurable, which is the per-constant remedy rather than the inventory; pm-tobi is CLOSED and set a destructive-default policy, a different axis; pm-z2j1qt is CLOSED and covered a single missing default bound on activity; pm-mfy1ux owns one command ignoring the row bound its siblings honour; pm-5t33or owns declared output budgets, which are one family within this population and whose values this item would label rather than choose; pm-m2il owns the scale conformance matrix that would let calibrated constants be re-fitted. Searched keyword and semantic for numeric constant, threshold, default, magic number, calibration; grepped the corpus for calibrat and magic number. No item owns the inventory or the labelling rule.

patch.value: Every numeric constant that affects runtime behaviour is declared as data with a unit, a provenance note, and exactly one label from invariant, calibrated, or arbitrary, and the declaration is machine-readable rather than a comment; A calibrated constant names the corpus it was fitted against and the procedure that would refit it, so a different installation can reproduce the fit rather than inherit the number; An arbitrary constant may govern a presentation default but may not be load-bearing on any correctness claim, and a test asserts that no arbitrary-labelled constant is read by a validation, integrity, or governance code path; A CI gate rejects a new numeric literal on a behavioural path that arrives without a label, so the population cannot grow while it is being dispositioned, with an explicit allowlist for build-gate thresholds that are out of scope and a recorded reason for each; The inventory states its own coverage: how many behavioural constants were found, how many carry each label, and which source areas were searched, so the residual is measurable rather than assumed complete; The three constants already known to be hazardous are labelled first and correctly: the recency weight that promotes every maintenance sweep, the worklist truncation that hides an actionable subset, and the golden-query set that certifies retrieval against one vocabulary

message: Acceptance criteria for the declared inventory, the labelling rule, the correctness prohibition, and the growth gate
